quiz.q: What observation does the Neo-Platonic proof begin from?
options: That things change from potential to actual
That abstract truths such as mathematical ones exist
That the things of our experience are made of parts
That the universe began to exist
quiz.explanation: The proof starts from composition. Change is chapter 1's starting point; abstract objects are chapter 3's; and the argument deliberately makes no claim about a beginning.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that a composite's dependence on its parts is fundamentally ‘atemporal’?
options: Because at every moment it exists, it needs its parts to exist and be united at that moment, whatever its history
Because every composite was assembled at some point in the past
Because time is an illusion on the Neo-Platonic view
Because composites exist outside time, like the One
quiz.explanation: The dependence holds moment by moment, even for a thing that always existed or came to be all at once. Past assembly is true of some composites (chairs) but not all (bodies), and it isn't the key point.

quiz.q: Which example does Feser use to show that a composite need not be assembled from pre-existing parts?
options: A chair made in a factory
A book glued together
A pile of stones
The human body, whose organs develop together in the womb
quiz.explanation: A body's arms, eyes, and organs develop together as cells divide; they are not first made and then put together. The chair is the example of something that *is* assembled.

quiz.q: Why can't a chair be the cause of its own parts' being united?
options: Because chairs are inanimate and lack a will
Because the chair's existence depends on that union, so making it the cause of the union creates an explanatory vicious circle
Because only God can cause anything at all
Because the chair's parts existed before the chair did
quiz.explanation: The whole exists only if the parts are united; if the whole also produced that union, each would depend on the other with nothing grounding either — ‘metaphysical bootstrapping’. Other things (screws, friction, bonds) really do cause, so the third option is wrong.

quiz.q: According to Feser, what is essential to a hierarchical (per se) causal series?
options: Its members all act at exactly the same instant
It stretches infinitely back in time
It involves only physical objects
Each member's causal power is derived from a prior member
quiz.explanation: Feser notes that the chair's sustaining causes happen to be simultaneous, but simultaneity is not what matters; derivation of causal power is (the stick moves the stone only because the hand moves it).

quiz.q: A friend says: ‘The worker who built this chair died years ago, yet it's still here — so the chair depends on no cause now.’ What is the best reply?
options: The worker's influence still lingers in the chair
True of the worker, who belongs to a linear series; but the chair still depends right now on screws, friction, molecular bonds and more — a hierarchical series
The chair will soon fall apart without the worker
Causation is always simultaneous, so the worker was never really a cause
quiz.explanation: The argument grants that linear causes can drop away. Its point is the hierarchical, here-and-now dependence of the chair on factors that must be operating for it to exist at this moment.

quiz.q: On the Aristotelian analysis Feser describes, what does matter contribute to a physical substance?
options: It ties a universal form down to a particular individual at a particular time and place
It gives the substance its distinctive properties and powers
It is the substance's existence as opposed to its essence
It is what makes the substance universal
quiz.explanation: Form accounts for kind and characteristic powers and is universal; matter individuates it. Essence/existence is a different (Thomist) distinction.

quiz.q: Why do form and matter require something outside them to account for their union?
options: Because form is always created before matter
Because matter resists being formed
Because Aristotle defined them that way
Because form without matter is a mere abstraction and matter without form is mere potentiality, so each depends on the other and neither can ground their union
quiz.explanation: Their mutual dependence would be a vicious circle unless something outside them accounts for their combination — the same structure as the chair and its parts.

quiz.q: What is Feser's attitude, in this chapter, toward the Aristotelian and Thomistic analyses of metaphysical parts?
options: The argument fails unless both are accepted
They are false but useful fictions
They are optional: the principle that composites need causes holds whatever the parts turn out to be
Only the essence/existence distinction is required
quiz.explanation: He says nothing rides on accepting them here; the point is that the principle is completely general. (He defends both theories elsewhere, and essence/existence returns in chapter 4.)

quiz.q: Why can't the first member of the hierarchical series be composite?
options: Because a composite would itself require a cause of its composition and so would not be first
Because composite things are always material
Because composite things cannot cause anything
Because the series must be infinite
quiz.explanation: Being first means having underived existence; anything with parts depends on something uniting them. Composites *can* cause things (screws do), so the third option misreads the argument.

quiz.q: How does Feser argue that there can be only one absolutely simple cause?
options: Two such causes would compete, and one would overpower the other
Ockham's razor tells us to posit only one
Two would need a differentiating feature, but having one would make each composite
Scripture teaches that there is only one God
quiz.explanation: A would be ‘simple cause plus F’ and B ‘simple cause plus G’ — composites. So nothing could distinguish two simple causes, and there cannot be two.

quiz.q: Why, according to the chapter, must the One be immutable?
options: Because change requires a body
Because it is eternal, and whatever is eternal cannot change
Because it is perfect, and perfect things never need to change
Because to change is to gain or lose a feature, which would make the One composite
quiz.explanation: Immutability is derived directly from simplicity. The order runs the other way from option 2: eternity is derived *from* immutability, not vice versa.

quiz.q: Which four-way classification of entities does Feser borrow from William Vallicella?
options: Substance, quality, quantity, relation
Mind, mental content, physical entity, abstract entity
God, angels, humans, animals
Form, matter, essence, existence
quiz.explanation: By eliminating abstract entities, physical entities, and mental contents, the argument concludes that the One is a mind or more like a mind than anything else.

quiz.q: Why can't the One be an abstract entity?
options: Abstract entities are causally inert, and the One is a cause
Abstract entities are composite
Abstract entities exist only in human minds
Abstract entities change over time
quiz.explanation: A stone can break a window; the pattern of being-a-stone cannot. Since the One causes the existence of composites, it isn't abstract.

quiz.q: According to Feser's footnote, how did Plotinus's own view differ from the chapter's conclusion?
options: Plotinus denied that the One is simple
Plotinus held that there are many Ones
Plotinus placed intellect in a second divine reality after the One
Plotinus thought the One was material
quiz.explanation: For Plotinus, Intellect (Nous) comes after the One. Feser, like later classical theists, concludes that the One itself is (or is most like) a mind — you can adopt the Neo-Platonic strategy without every detail.

quiz.q: How does the chapter move from the One's simplicity to its pure actuality?
options: Pure actuality is simply part of the definition of ‘the One’
Because the One is eternal, it cannot have potential
Because the One resembles the Unmoved Mover
It must be at least partly actual to cause anything, and a mixture of actuality and potentiality would be a composition
quiz.explanation: Steps 33–34: an actual ‘part’ plus a potential ‘part’ would be composite; having no parts, the One is purely actual.

quiz.q: Why does Feser conclude that the One and the Unmoved Mover are identical?
options: Because Plotinus and Aristotle agreed with each other
Because both are purely actual, and there cannot be more than one purely actual being
Because both are the earliest cause in time
Because both are traditionally called ‘God’
quiz.explanation: Chapter 1 showed that pure actuality can't be multiplied; chapter 2 shows the One is purely actual. Different starting points, same reality.

quiz.q: Someone objects: ‘If God is omnipotent and omniscient, those are two properties, so God has parts.’ Which reply follows Feser's first line of response?
options: The two expressions differ in sense but refer to one simple reality, as ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ both refer to Venus
Omnipotence and omniscience are only metaphors
God has parts, but they are immaterial
Omniscience is really a kind of omnipotence, so there is only one property
quiz.explanation: Frege's sense/reference distinction: different meanings, one referent. Feser's follow-up is analogical predication; he never says the attributes are metaphorical.

quiz.q: Which pair illustrates an analogical (rather than univocal or equivocal) use of a term?
options: ‘Rover is a dog’ / ‘Fido is a dog’
‘The batter swung the bat’ / ‘A bat flew around the attic’
‘Venus is the morning star’ / ‘Venus is the evening star’
‘The wine is good’ / ‘George is a good man’
quiz.explanation: ‘Dog’ is univocal (same sense); ‘bat’ is equivocal (unrelated senses); ‘good’ of wine and of a man is analogical (related but different senses). The Venus pair illustrates sense/reference, not analogy.

quiz.q: What role does wave–particle duality play in the chapter?
options: It is offered as evidence that God exists
It shows that physics conflicts with divine simplicity
It illustrates why stretching concepts to remote realities should be expected to yield hard-to-grasp conclusions
It is an example of a composite that has no cause
quiz.explanation: The analogy defuses the charge that simplicity is suspiciously strange: we accept strange conclusions in physics when evidence demands them in domains remote from experience, and the ground of reality is more remote still.

quiz.q: A critic says: ‘The unity of a thing's parts is just a brute fact.’ What is Feser's key response?
options: Brute facts are impossible by definition
Then the critic gives no explanation rather than an alternative one, and has no non-question-begging reason to reject the explanation already offered
Science will eventually explain the unity
The composite causes its own unity
quiz.explanation: Feser (with Gerson) stresses that a brute fact is not a rival explanation. The self-causation option is the incoherent alternative he rejects.

quiz.q: A student proposes that a special ‘binding part’ C unites a thing's parts A and B. What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing; this is Feser's own view
C would have to be God
A thing can have only two parts
C would itself need to be united with A and B, starting a regress that multiplies rather than solves the problem
quiz.explanation: Following Vallicella: each new unifying part is one more item needing to be unified with the rest.

quiz.q: Why doesn't an appeal to the laws of nature end the regress, according to Feser?
options: A, B, and the law together form a further composite whose unity needs explaining — and on the Aristotelian view laws presuppose form–matter composition
Laws of nature do not exist
Science cannot study composition
Laws are mental contents and so cannot be ultimate
quiz.explanation: We must ask why A and B obey *that* law; the package is a new composite. And if laws describe how substantial forms operate, they presuppose the composition they were meant to explain.

quiz.q: Which statement best explains why ‘What caused God?’ misfires against this argument?
options: Because God is too great to be caused
Because the argument assumes the universe had a beginning
Because the argument claims only that composites need causes, and something absolutely simple has nothing to unite, so it could not have a cause
Because God caused himself
quiz.explanation: The principle is not ‘everything has a cause’. God isn't an arbitrary exception; the principle applies only to what has parts. Self-causation is exactly the incoherence Feser rejects.

quiz.q: A physicist suggests that the ultimate cause is a single fundamental field with no smaller parts. By the chapter's reasoning, what is the problem?
options: Fields are abstract and so causally inert
A field has structure, varying values, and a nature distinct from its existence, so it is still composite
Nothing — a field with no smaller parts would be the One
Fields are mental contents
quiz.explanation: ‘Parts’ in this argument include structural and metaphysical composition, not just smaller pieces. Chapter 7 applies this reasoning to the universe and the laws of physics.

shortAnswer.q: Explain the two senses in which parts and wholes can each be ‘more fundamental’, and say which one the argument relies on.
shortAnswer.model: In one sense the whole is prior: we understand a part by its function in the whole (a leg is for walking, an eye for seeing, a cover for protecting pages). In another sense the parts are prior: the whole cannot exist unless its parts exist and are put together correctly (a heap of chair parts, or the same parts made into a table, is not a chair). The argument relies on the second, existential sense.
rubric: States the whole's priority for understanding, with an example
States the parts' priority for existence, with an example
Mentions that correct arrangement matters, not just the parts' existence
Identifies the existential sense as the one the argument uses

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser insist that a composite's dependence on its parts is atemporal? Use his examples.
shortAnswer.model: Past assembly is only sometimes true: chairs are built from pre-made pieces, but a body's organs develop together in the womb. More importantly, even a chair that always existed, or that came into being all at once, would still need its parts existing and united at each moment. So the fundamental dependence is moment by moment. This means the argument concerns a present sustaining cause and is indifferent to whether the universe had a beginning.
rubric: Distinguishes temporal (assembly) from atemporal (moment-by-moment) dependence
Uses the body example
Uses the eternal or instantaneous chair example
Draws the implication about the universe's beginning

shortAnswer.q: Why must the cause of a composite's unity be something outside the composite? Address the options of self-causation, a further part, and brute fact.
shortAnswer.model: Self-causation is incoherent: the composite's existence depends on its parts being united, so it cannot also produce that union without a vicious circle (bootstrapping). A further part C only relocates the question — what unites C with A and B? — and generates a regress of unifiers. Declaring the union a brute fact offers no explanation at all rather than an alternative one, and (as Gerson notes) ‘maybe there's no explanation’ is no reason to reject the explanation already given. So the cause must be external.
rubric: Explains the vicious circle of self-causation
Explains the regress of further parts
Explains why a brute fact is not an alternative explanation
Mentions that the Neo-Platonic explanation remains unrefuted (Gerson's point)

shortAnswer.q: How do form/matter and essence/existence count as ‘parts’, and why do they too need a cause of their union?
shortAnswer.model: For Aristotelians, a physical substance is form (which gives it its kind and powers and is universal) plus matter (which individuates it). Form without matter is an abstraction; matter without form is mere potential. For Thomists, a thing is also its essence (what it is) plus its existence (that it is); existence is always the existence of some kind of thing, while the essence alone is an abstraction. In each case the two depend on one another, so without an outside cause of their union there would be a vicious circle. Feser adds that the argument doesn't require these theories; they show how general the principle is.
rubric: Correctly characterizes form and matter
Correctly characterizes essence and existence
Explains the mutual dependence and resulting circle
Notes that the argument does not depend on accepting these theories

shortAnswer.q: Why must the hierarchical series of causes of composition terminate in something absolutely simple?
shortAnswer.model: Each member of a hierarchical series has only derived causal power, like the stick moved by the hand; without a first member whose power isn't derived, there would be no causal activity at all (chapter 1). The first member cannot be composite, because a composite needs a cause of its composition and so would not be first. So it must have no parts of any kind — physical or metaphysical.
rubric: Explains derivative power in a hierarchical series
Explains why an unending hierarchical series would explain nothing
Explains why a composite cannot be first
Specifies that simplicity rules out metaphysical as well as physical parts

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct Feser's argument that there can be only one absolutely simple cause.
shortAnswer.model: If there were two, A and B, they would have to differ: A would have some feature F that B lacks, and B some feature G that A lacks. But then A would be ‘simple cause plus F’ and B ‘simple cause plus G’ — each a composite of what it shares with the other and what distinguishes it. A truly simple cause has no parts, so it cannot have a distinguishing feature. So there is nothing to differentiate two simple causes, and there can be only one. The One is ‘one’ as both partless and unique.
rubric: States that plurality requires a differentiating feature
Shows that such a feature would make each composite
Concludes that there is only one
Notes the two senses of ‘one’

shortAnswer.q: How does the chapter argue that the One is a mind, and how does this depart from Plotinus?
shortAnswer.model: Following Vallicella, everything is a mind, a mental content, a physical thing, or an abstract thing. The One is not abstract, because abstractions are causally inert (the pattern of a stone can't break a window) and the One is a cause. It is not physical, because physical things have parts and can come to be and pass away. It is not a mental content, because thoughts depend on minds and so cannot be ultimate. So it is a mind, or more like a mind than anything else. Plotinus placed intellect in a second reality after the One; Feser keeps the general Neo-Platonic approach but not this detail.
rubric: States the fourfold classification
Gives the reason for each elimination
Notes Vallicella's hedged conclusion
Explains the difference from Plotinus

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser hold that the One is identical with chapter 1's Unmoved Mover?
shortAnswer.model: The One must be at least partly actual in order to cause anything, since the merely potential can do nothing; but if it had potential as well as actuality, it would be composite. So it is purely actual. Chapter 1 showed that there cannot be more than one purely actual being, since there would be nothing to differentiate two. So the One and the Unmoved Mover are the same reality, reached by different routes: parts/whole versus act/potency.
rubric: Derives pure actuality from simplicity
Cites the uniqueness of pure actuality from chapter 1
Concludes identity
Frames the two proofs as different routes to one summit

shortAnswer.q: Answer the objection that the One's many attributes would give it many parts.
shortAnswer.model: First, using Frege's sense/reference distinction: ‘omnipotent’ and ‘intellect’ differ in meaning, yet they can refer to one reality, as ‘the morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ both refer to Venus. Second, if pressed that in humans power and intellect really are distinct features: that would carry over only if the terms were used univocally of God. Because the One is simple, they are used analogically — in related but not identical senses, like ‘good’ of wine and of a man, and still literally. There is in God something analogous to our power and intellect, but in him they are one reality. Third, such strangeness is to be expected, as with wave–particle duality.
rubric: Uses sense/reference with the Venus example
Distinguishes univocal, equivocal, and analogical use
Stresses that analogical is literal, not metaphorical
Explains why the result being hard to grasp is expected

shortAnswer.q: Why can't the laws of nature provide an alternative explanation of why a composite's parts are united?
shortAnswer.model: Any law-based explanation leaves a new composite to explain. If it is a law that things of type A and type B combine under certain conditions, we must ask why A and B are governed by that law rather than another; A, B, and the law together are a further complex whose unity needs explaining, so the regress continues. On the Aristotelian view, laws are descriptions of how things behave given their substantial forms; but substantial form is one of the two principles (with prime matter) the thing is composed of, so laws presuppose composition rather than explaining it.
rubric: Explains the ‘why this law?’ question
Identifies A, B, and the law as a further composite
Presents the Aristotelian footnote point
Concludes that only something simple ends the regress

shortAnswer.q: Why does ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ fail against this argument?
shortAnswer.model: The argument never says everything has a cause; it says whatever is composite has a cause of its composition. Something absolutely simple has nothing to be united, so it not only needs no cause but could not have one. This isn't special pleading or an ad hoc dodge: it follows from the very principle the argument uses and was the Neo-Platonic view from the start. And the universe can't be the uncaused thing, because it is composite.
rubric: Correctly states the argument's actual principle
Explains why a simple being could not be caused
Rebuts the charge of ad hoc special pleading
Explains why the universe can't fill the role

flashcards.front: Starting point of the Neo-Platonic proof
flashcards.back: The things of our experience are composite — made up of parts.
Whole prior to parts for understanding (parts defined by function); parts prior to whole for existence (whole needs parts existing and rightly arranged).
At every moment a composite exists, it needs its parts united at that moment — even if it always existed or came to be all at once.

flashcards.front: Feser's example of a composite that was never assembled
flashcards.back: The human body: its organs develop together as cells divide in the womb.

flashcards.front: Why a composite can't cause its own composition
flashcards.back: Its existence depends on the union of its parts, so making it the cause of that union is an explanatory vicious circle — ‘metaphysical bootstrapping’.

flashcards.front: What sustains the chair right now?
flashcards.back: Screws, friction, molecular and atomic bonds, a suitable room temperature — many factors combined at that moment.

flashcards.front: Linear vs. hierarchical causes of the chair
flashcards.back: Linear: the worker who assembled it long ago. Hierarchical: the factors holding it together now, each with derived causal power.

flashcards.front: What is essential to a hierarchical series?
flashcards.back: Derived causal power (the stick moves the stone only because the hand moves it) — not simultaneity as such.
The universal principle that makes a thing the kind it is and gives it its powers (copper's conductivity, a tree's roots, an animal's senses).
What ties a universal form down to a particular individual here and now; alone it is mere potentiality.

flashcards.front: Why form and matter need an external cause
flashcards.back: Form alone is an abstraction; matter alone is mere potential. Each depends on the other, so their union needs a cause outside them.
What a thing is (triangle: closed plane figure with three straight sides) vs. that it is (this triangle's existence).
Whatever is composite has a cause — whatever kind of parts it has.

flashcards.front: Why the first member must be simple
flashcards.back: Any composite member would need a cause of its composition and so would not be first.
No parts of any kind: no physical parts, no form/matter, no essence/existence, no act/potency, no bearer/feature distinction.
Plotinus (c. 204/5–270 AD), founder of Neo-Platonism, author of the Enneads.
The One (the Good), Intellect (Nous), Soul — everything flowing from the One.
Two simple causes would need a differentiating feature; having one would make each composite; so there is only one.
Change is gaining or losing a feature; a thing that could do so would be the thing plus the feature — composite.

flashcards.front: Two senses in which the One is eternal
flashcards.back: Outside time (because changeless) and without beginning or end (no parts to be combined or dissolved).
Whatever is caused has parts needing combination; the One has none — so it could not have a cause.
Everything is a mind, a mental content, a physical entity, or an abstract entity.
Abstract entities are causally inert (the pattern of a stone can't break a window); the One is a cause.

flashcards.front: Why the One isn't a mental content
flashcards.back: A thought depends on the mind that thinks it, so it can't be an ultimate cause.
Plotinus put intellect in a second reality after the One; Feser concludes the One is itself a mind (or more like a mind than anything else).

flashcards.front: Why the One is purely actual
flashcards.back: It must be actual to cause anything; a mixture of actual and potential would be a composition; it has no parts.
Perfect, omnipotent, fully good, omniscient — via pure actuality and proportionate causality.

flashcards.front: Relation of the One to the Unmoved Mover
flashcards.back: Identical: both are purely actual, and there can be only one purely actual being.
Sense = how an expression presents its object; reference = the object. ‘Morning star’ and ‘evening star’: different senses, one referent (Venus).
Same sense (‘dog’) / unrelated senses (‘bat’) / related but different senses (‘good’ wine, ‘good’ man).
No. It is literal: wine and George are both literally good, in analogous senses.

flashcards.front: Why strangeness of the conclusion is expected
flashcards.back: Like wave–particle duality, concepts stretched far from everyday experience yield hard-to-grasp results; the ground of reality is farthest of all.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘a further part unites the parts’
flashcards.back: What unites that part with the others? The regress multiplies the problem rather than solving it (Vallicella).
That's no explanation, not an alternative one; and ‘maybe there's no explanation’ is no reason to reject the explanation offered (Gerson).

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘laws of nature explain composition’
flashcards.back: Parts plus the law form a further composite (why this law?); and on the Aristotelian view laws presuppose form–matter composition.
The premise is not ‘everything has a cause’ but ‘whatever is composite has a cause’; the absolutely simple neither needs nor could have one.

teachBack:
**Your challenge:** explain the Neo-Platonic proof out loud, in under ten minutes, to someone who has never studied philosophy — a friend, a sibling, or an imagined skeptical coworker. Use only one physical prop (a chair, a pen, or your phone) and no jargon until the listener has agreed to Stage 1.

**Constraints:**

1. Get your listener to agree, in their own words, that the object needs its parts united *right now* and cannot unite them itself.
2. Explain why the chain of ‘what holds this together?’ has to stop, using the stick-and-stone idea rather than the phrase ‘per se series’.
3. Name at least two kinds of parts that are not physical pieces (form/matter, essence/existence, or actual/potential).
4. Derive at least three attributes from simplicity, saying ‘because it has no parts’ each time.
5. Field one objection — ideally ‘What caused God?’ or ‘physics explains it’ — and answer it in two sentences.

**Check yourself afterwards:**

- Did you ever say ‘everything has a cause’? (If so, you gave away the argument.)
- Did you ever imply the argument is about the Big Bang or the past?
- Could your listener repeat back why there can only be one simple cause?
- Could you explain, if asked, how the One relates to chapter 1's Unmoved Mover?
- Where did you hesitate or hand-wave? Reread those parts of the summary and the Argument steps, then try again with a different listener.
videoPrompt: Audience: curious adults with no philosophy background, some skeptical of religion. Explain Edward Feser's Neo-Platonic proof. Emphasize, in order: (1) everything we experience is made of parts and exists only while they are united; (2) this dependence is here and now — even an eternal chair would need it; (3) nothing holds itself together, and a ‘binding part’, a brute fact, or the laws of nature don't end the question; (4) the chain must end in something with no parts, the One, named after Plotinus; (5) simplicity yields uniqueness, changelessness, eternity, intellect, pure actuality; (6) this is the Unmoved Mover of chapter 1. Use the chair, the heap of parts, the overheated room, and ‘morning star/evening star’. Correct the myths that the argument says ‘everything has a cause’ or needs a beginning of the universe. Tone: clear, warm, serious, never preachy.
